claims.text: Introducing a controlled amount of grain-boundary-pinning particles, such as oxide nanoparticles, will preserve the toughness of the high-entropy alloy after thermal exposure and loading.
The initial high-entropy alloy is a single-phase solid solution.
Oxide nanoparticles can serve as grain-boundary-pinning particles in the alloy.
The applicable regime is exposure at 700°C for 1000 hours followed by quasi-static tensile loading at a strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1.
Thermal aging at 700°C can produce phase segregation or precipitate formation in a solid-solution high-entropy alloy.
Grain-boundary-pinning particles will inhibit grain growth during thermal exposure.
Grain-boundary-pinning particles will prevent formation of detrimental phases during thermal exposure.
The detrimental phase that may be prevented is the sigma phase.
Inhibiting grain growth and detrimental-phase formation will preserve toughness.
After identical exposure and loading, the particle-containing alloy will have higher toughness than the same alloy without particles.
The appropriate baseline is the same high-entropy alloy without grain-boundary-pinning particles, tested under identical conditions.
Grain size, phase composition, and mechanical properties will be monitored.
The optimal amount and type of pinning particles remain uncertain.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing particle-containing and particle-free versions of the alloy after 700°C exposure for 1000 hours using quasi-static tensile testing.
Lower toughness in the particle-containing alloy than in the particle-free control under identical conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
